doc.title: Paul Shaffer interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, August 24, 2023

title: Summer arranging course and bar band in Toronto
summary: He stayed in Toronto the summer to take an arranging course and played in a bar band, then met a guitarist in Yorkville.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: I’ve got time if you do.

Have to do a commercial? All right well ‘cause this is where the moment where I realized something had to change. First of all I didn’t really go home for the summer after my first year at the University of Toronto because there was music happening in Toronto. I just had to stay. And I told my parents, of course I visited them at the beginning and the end of the summer but in the middle I said I would like to stay in Toronto and take a course in arranging. It was really that Blood, Sweat & Tears influence hipping me to the whole concept of arranging. “I’d like to take a course” and I knew I could sell them on this, just that word “course” that they were going to go for it and they did. They allowed me to stay in Toronto and it was very easy for me to get a job there in a bar band, live music in bars, which we had kind of the tail end of that scene that the Robbie Robertson and The Band came out of. I did that for the summer with some older guys and it’s lucky I did take that course in arranging, it’s the only real training I had in arranging. But, and it paid off. I certainly used it later on. I knew how to write a chart and did a little bit, even up in Toronto. So you know I may have been at some all-night jam session or something coming home late about 6 AM walking through — Toronto had its own Greenwich Village kind of place called Yorkville Village, and I walked by a guy at 6 AM sitting on a stoop in front of — he had a little deli grocery store kind of place, playing acoustic guitar, and I walked by him and then my ear caught what he was doing, I never heard anything like that, and I listened to him for a while. And he was a sort of a, you know we were all hippie styled looking guys at the time. He was a little Latin looking to me. And I said, “What are you doing? What the hell is that?” And he said, “Well are you a player?” And I said, “Well I play a little piano but I don’t know anything about what you’re doing and it’s just so intriguing.” And he said, “Well is there a piano?” I said, “Well over at the dorm you know, there’s a practice room.” We went over there, by now it’s 8 AM and he starts to show me some things that really opened me up, my ears up, starting with standards, you know things that I knew through my parents and their love of music and jazz and stuff but I couldn’t hear those kind of voicings at all. He immediately showed me a few things that started opening those things up to me. And then I started playing with him and apprenticing with him. And the second year of college I was now playing on the side with this guy, whose name was Michael Munoz.
